general
graded

<2 mm

questions.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features

opts: Spirometry alone, without symptoms
Symptoms (cough) plus CT for confirmation
Symptoms (dyspnea) plus spirometry for confirmation
Symptoms (dyspnea) plus chest X-ray for confirmation

questions.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features

High birth weight (post-term)
Low birth weight (Pre terms)
Occupational dust
questions.exp: The risk list prints 'Low birth weight (Pre terms)' with tobacco smoking, cooking-fuel smoke, occupational dust, vapours, fumes and other chemicals; high birth weight is not on it. (Book p267)

questions.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features

opts: Dyspnea, chronic cough, clubbing and wheeze
Fever, chronic cough, recurrent lower respiratory tract infection and wheeze
Dyspnea, hemoptysis, recurrent lower respiratory tract infection and wheeze
Dyspnea, chronic cough, recurrent lower respiratory tract infection and wheeze
questions.exp: The list is 'Dyspnea', 'Chronic cough', 'Recurrent lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI)' and 'wheeze'; hemoptysis and clubbing are not part of it. (Book p267)

questions.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features

opts: exertion
lying flat
inspiration
cold air
questions.exp: Under dyspnea the page writes 'Persistent progressive' and 'Aggravating factor: Exertion', while the cough is described as intermittent with ± sputum production. (Book p267)

questions.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features

False — cough is not listed among the clinical features of COPD
False — the cough is paroxysmal and always dry
True — the cough is intermittent and may or may not produce sputum
questions.exp: The cough bullets are 'Intermittent' and '± sputum production', the ± sign carrying the optional sputum. (Book p267)

questions.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features

A normal FEV₁/FVC but a reduced DLCO
Chest X-ray hyperinflation plus symptoms, spirometry being optional
Symptoms of dyspnea plus spirometry for confirmation, with post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7
questions.exp: The diagnosis line is 'Symptoms (Dyspnea) + Spirometry (For confirmation)', and page 271 adds the post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.7 that confirms airflow obstruction. (Book p267)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease

opts: A clinical disease defined by cough with sputum ≥3 months/year for ≥2 years
A pathological disease defined by dilatation of airway distal to the terminal bronchiole
A clinical disease defined by cough with sputum ≥2 months/year for ≥3 years
A physiological disease defined by reduced FEV1/FVC with hyperinflation
questions.exp: The definition cell reads 'Clinical disease: Cough with sputum ≥3 months/year for ≥2 years' — the mirror image of the emphysema cell, which is pathological. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
questions.q: Which duration pair defines chronic bronchitis in the table?
opts: ≥2 months per year for ≥3 years
≥3 months per year for ≥2 years
≥3 months per year for ≥3 years
≥6 months per year for ≥2 years
questions.exp: The cell prints 'Cough with sputum ≥3 months/year for ≥2 years', the standard clinical definition placed under the 'Clinical disease' heading. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
questions.q: Which definition of emphysema is printed beside chronic bronchitis on page 268?
opts: A pathological disease: fibrosis of the alveolar interstitium with honeycomb change
A pathological disease: dilatation of airway proximal to the terminal bronchiole with intact alveolar walls
A pathological disease: dilatation of airway distal to the terminal bronchiole followed by destruction of wall and air spaces
A clinical disease: cough with sputum for ≥3 months/year for ≥2 years
questions.exp: The emphysema cell is 'Pathological disease: Dilatation of airway distal to terminal bronchiole followed by destruction of wall & air spaces' — destruction is the operative word. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
questions.q: Match each disease to its printed pathology — 1) Chronic bronchitis 2) Emphysema … A) Small airway disease of the abnormal alveolo-capillary unit, minimal parenchymal damage, exhale CO₂ and ↓ elastic recoil B) Large airway disease plus parenchymal destruction
questions.exp: The pathology row gives chronic bronchitis 'Large airway disease + parenchymal destruction' and emphysema 'Small airway disease: Abnormal alveolo-capillary unit (Affects diffusion)', minimal parenchymal damage with CO₂ exhalation and reduced elastic recoil. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
questions.q: Match each disease to its printed age band — 1) Chronic bronchitis 2) Emphysema … A) 50–75 years (elderly) B) 40–45 years
questions.exp: The age row reads 40–45 years for chronic bronchitis and 50–75 years (elderly) for emphysema. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
questions.q: Which chain produces the blue bloater picture in the chronic bronchitis column?
opts: Cough with copious sputum, type I respiratory failure with ↓PaO₂ and ↓PaCO₂, and left ventricular failure
Severe dyspnea with ↑ work of breathing → ↓PCO₂, cachexia, Hoover sign and type I respiratory failure
Cough with copious sputum, hyperinflation with ↑AP diameter and a small heart
Cough with copious sputum, hypoxia → cyanosis, right ventricle failure → edema, type II respiratory failure with ↓PaO₂ and ↑PaCO₂, and cor pulmonale with RV hypertrophy/dilatation ± failure
questions.exp: The blue bloater branch prints hypoxia → cyanosis and RV failure → edema, then type II failure '↓PaO2 ↑PaCO2' and cor pulmonale 'RV hypertrophy/dilatation ± failure', with infections listed as well. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
questions.q: Which cluster belongs to the pink puffer column of the table?
opts: Severe dyspnea, ↑ work of breathing → ↓PCO₂, cachectic, Hoover sign, hyper resonance, pursed lips and type I respiratory failure
Cough with copious sputum, cyanosis, edema and type II respiratory failure
Mild dyspnea, hyper resonance, cor pulmonale and type II respiratory failure
Severe dyspnea, ↑ work of breathing → ↑PCO₂, obesity and type II respiratory failure
questions.exp: The emphysema column lists severe dyspnea, ↑ work of breathing → ↓PCO₂, cachectic, Hoover sign, hyper resonance, pursed lips and type I respiratory failure — the mirror image of the blue bloater. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
questions.q: Match each disease to its printed chest X-ray — 1) Chronic bronchitis 2) Emphysema … A) Hyperinflation of lung (AP diameter ↑) and small heart B) Prominent vessels and large heart
questions.exp: The CXR row gives prominent vessels and a large heart for chronic bronchitis against hyperinflation with increased AP diameter and a small heart for emphysema. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
questions.q: Match each disease to its printed pulmonary function — 1) Chronic bronchitis 2) Emphysema … A) TLC and RV increased with DLCO decreased B) TLC normal with DLCO normal
questions.exp: The PFT row reads TLC normal and DLCO normal for chronic bronchitis, while emphysema raises TLC and RV and lowers DLCO. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease

tertiary
respiratory
primary

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
questions.q: Which structures make up the respiratory unit of the lung in the printed note?
opts: The respiratory bronchiole and the pulmonary capillary bed, without alveoli
Everything distal to the secondary pulmonary lobule — alveolar duct → alveoli only
The terminal bronchiole with its cartilage and the alveoli
Everything distal to the terminal bronchiole — respiratory bronchiole → alveolar duct → alveoli
questions.exp: The note reads 'Respiratory unit of lung: Distal to terminal bronchiole (Respiratory bronchiole → Alveolar duct → Alveoli)', the arrow sequence being the tested part. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease

Most common, seen in smokers, and involves the upper lobe of lung
Most common, seen in non-smokers, and involves the lower lobe of lung
Rare, seen in young male smokers, and associated with spontaneous pneumothorax
questions.exp: The centriacinar row lists 'most common', 'seen in smokers' and 'involve upper lobe of lung' beside the diagram of respiratory bronchiole involvement. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease

False — chronic bronchitis requires a reduced DLCO for diagnosis
True — cough with sputum for at least 2 months a year for 3 consecutive years defines it clinically
False — chronic bronchitis is defined pathologically by airspace destruction
questions.exp: The definition cell reads 'Clinical disease: Cough with sputum ≥3 months/year for ≥2 years', while DLCO is normal in chronic bronchitis and destruction of airspaces defines emphysema. (Book p268)

questions.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
questions.q: Which four features are printed for panacinar (entire acinus) emphysema?

Age >45 years, seen in smokers, involves the upper lobe, and is associated with spontaneous pneumothorax
Age <45 years, seen in non-smokers, involves the lower lobe (basilar), and is associated with vasculitis, liver disease and bronchiectasis from α-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Young male smoker, involves the lower lobe, and is associated with spontaneous pneumothorax
questions.exp: The panacinar row reads 'Age <45 years', 'Seen in non-smokers', 'Involve lower lobe of lung (Basilar)' and 'Associated with vasculitis, liver disease, bronchiectasis (α-1 antitrypsin deficiency)'. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
questions.q: Which two features are printed for paraseptal emphysema?
opts: Elderly female non-smoker and associated with vasculitis
Young male smoker and associated with α-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Non-smoker below 45 years and involves the basilar lower lobe
Young male smoker and associated with spontaneous pneumothorax
questions.exp: The paraseptal row has only two cells filled — 'Young male smoker' and 'Associated with spontaneous pneumothorax' — with the diagram showing subpleural alveolar ducts and alveoli. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note

upper lobe involvement
smoker status
α-1 antitrypsin deficiency

questions.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
questions.q: Which protease-antiprotease pathway is drawn on page 269?
opts: α-1 antitrypsin inhibits neutrophil elastase, which otherwise destroys extracellular matrix, and the protein is encoded by the SERPINA-1 gene
α-1 antitrypsin activates neutrophil elastase, which then destroys extracellular matrix, and the protein is encoded by the SERPINA-1 gene
Neutrophil elastase inhibits α-1 antitrypsin, which otherwise destroys extracellular matrix, and the protein is encoded by the SERPINA-1 gene
α-1 antitrypsin inhibits neutrophil elastase, which otherwise destroys extracellular matrix, and the protein is encoded by the alpha-1 globulin gene
questions.exp: The flow reads 'α-1 antitrypsin ↓Inhibit Neutrophil elastase' over the arrow 'SERPINA-1 gene → Extracellular matrix destruction', i.e. antitrypsin restrains elastase. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
questions.q: α-1 antitrypsin, the inhibitor of neutrophil elastase, is encoded by the ______ gene.
opts: SERPINB-1
SERPINA-1
SERPINC-1
SERPINE-1
questions.exp: The label under the enzyme in the flow diagram reads 'SERPINA-1 gene', naming the gene before the arrow to extracellular matrix destruction. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
questions.q: Which statement of the protease-antiprotease theory is printed on page 269?
opts: Deficiency of neutrophil elastase raises α-1 antitrypsin activity
Excess of α-1 antitrypsin raises neutrophil elastase activity
Deficiency of α-1 antitrypsin lowers neutrophil elastase activity
Deficiency of α-1 antitrypsin raises neutrophil elastase activity
questions.exp: The theory bullet reads 'Deficiency of α-1 antitrypsin: ↑ neutrophil elastase activity', from which the matrix destruction and panacinar pattern follow. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
questions.q: Match each genotype to its printed meaning — 1) PiMM 2) PiZZ … A) Disease (+) and the most common form of α-1 antitrypsin deficiency B) Normal
questions.exp: The genetics block lists the m, Z and Null alleles, then 'PiMM: Normal' and 'PiZZ: Disease (+) (m/c form of α-1 antitrypsin deficiency)'. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are printed under spontaneous pneumothorax on page 269, one is not:
opts: Centriacinar emphysema
Lymphangioma hematosis
Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Paraseptal emphysema
questions.exp: The note lists paraseptal change, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and 'Lymphangioma hematosis' as printed. Centriacinar disease belongs to the smoker's upper-lobe pattern, not this list. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
questions.q: A 38-year-old non-smoker has basilar emphysema with a history of liver disease and bronchiectasis. Which printed emphysema type and enzyme defect fit?
opts: Irregular emphysema with neutrophil elastase excess
Panacinar emphysema with α-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Centriacinar emphysema with α-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Paraseptal emphysema with α-1 antitrypsin deficiency
questions.exp: Panacinar disease occurs below 45 years in non-smokers, in the basilar lower lobe, and is 'Associated with vasculitis, liver disease, bronchiectasis (α-1 antitrypsin deficiency)'. (Book p269)

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: Which set of large-airway changes is printed for chronic bronchitis on page 270?
opts: Neutrophils in sputum, squamous metaplasia of epithelium, basement membrane thickening, and a severe increase in airway smooth muscle giving hyperresponsive symptoms

Neutrophils in sputum, squamous metaplasia of epithelium, no basement membrane thickening, ↑ macrophages, ↑ CD8+ lymphocytes, goblet cell hyperplasia with mucous hypersecretion, and little increase in airway smooth muscle giving no hyperresponsive symptoms
Eosinophils in sputum, epithelial necrosis, basement membrane thickening and severe bronchospasm
Neutrophils in sputum, goblet cell hyperplasia, and loss of cartilage with airway collapse
questions.exp: The diagram labels all of those large-airway features and ends 'Little increase in airway smooth muscle → No hyperresponsive symptoms', which is the point separating it from asthma. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: Match each feature to the asthma column of the note table — 1) Bronchospasm 2) Necrosis of epithelium 3) Squamous metaplasia 4) Mucus secretion … A) Severe (↑ airway smooth muscle) B) Present C) Absent D) Increased

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: In the note table, necrosis of epithelium is ______ in chronic bronchitis and present in asthma.
opts: mild
severe
absent
focal
questions.exp: The chronic bronchitis column reads bronchospasm mild, mucus secretion increased, necrosis of epithelium absent and squamous metaplasia present. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: Which changes are labelled in the small airway diagram of emphysema?
opts: Inflammatory exudate in the lumen, a wall thickened by inflammatory cells, macrophages, CD8+ cells and fibroblasts, peribronchial fibrosis, a lymphoid follicle and disrupted alveolar attachments
Squamous metaplasia, goblet cell hyperplasia and neutrophils in the sputum
Inflammatory exudate in the lumen with an intact alveolar attachment and no fibrosis
Basement membrane thickening, eosinophils and severe bronchospasm
questions.exp: The small airway diagram labels inflammatory exudate in the lumen, thickened wall with inflammatory cells, macrophages, CD8+ cells and fibroblast, peribronchial fibrosis, lymphoid follicle and disrupted alveolar attachments; squamous metaplasia and goblet hyperplasia belong to the large airway panel. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: Which consequence follows the disrupted alveolar attachments in emphysema?
opts: ↓ ERP → alveoli collapse → reduced lung volumes with ↓ TLC and ↓ RV
↑ ERP → airway collapse → air trapping with normal TLC and RV
↓ ERP → alveoli are easily inflatable → hyperinflated lung with ↑ TLC and ↑ RV
↑ ERP → alveoli are stiff → restrictive lung with ↓ TLC and ↓ RV
questions.exp: The arrows read 'Disrupted alveolar attachments → ↓ ERP → Alveoli are easily inflatable → Hyperinflated lung (↑ TLC, ↑ RV)'. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: The driving pressure of exhalation is printed as DP = intrapleural pressure (IPP) + ______ pressure (ERP).
opts: airway
elastic recoil
transpulmonary
alveolar
questions.exp: The physiology line reads 'DP = Intrapleural pressure (IPP) + elastic recoil pressure (ERP)', and forceful exhalation then raises IPP while lowering ERP. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: What happens to driving pressure during forceful exhalation, and why?
opts: It falls below airway pressure because IPP falls and ERP rises
It stays equal to airway pressure because IPP and ERP change in parallel
It rises above airway pressure because IPP rises and ERP falls
It falls below airway pressure because IPP rises and ERP falls
questions.exp: The page writes 'Forceful exhalation: ↑ IPP, ↓ ERP → DP < AP', the fall in driving pressure being the mechanism of dynamic airway compression. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: Why do the bronchi but not the distal airways resist collapse in emphysema?
opts: The bronchi have no cartilage and collapse, whereas the distal airways are held open by elastic recoil
Cartilage is present at the bronchi and prevents collapse, whereas airways collapse, trap air and raise the work of breathing
Both bronchi and distal airways are cartilaginous, but only the distal airways trap air
Cartilage is present at the bronchi, and the distal airways are held open by surfactant
questions.exp: The two bullets read 'At bronchi → Cartilage present (Prevents collapse)' and 'At airways → Collapse → Air trapping → ↑ work of breathing → Dyspnea'. (Book p270)

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are large-airway features of chronic bronchitis on page 270, one belongs to asthma:
opts: Severe increase in airway smooth muscle
Goblet cell hyperplasia
Squamous metaplasia of epithelium
Neutrophils in sputum

questions.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three are printed as small airway changes of emphysema on page 270, one belongs to the large airway panel:

Peribronchial fibrosis
Inflammatory exudate in the lumen
Lymphoid follicle

questions.sec: The Alveolar DLCO Split, the Hypoxia to Cor Pulmonale Chain, Emphysematous PFT with Reversibility Testing, the GOLD Grades and the ABE Tool

opts: Parenchyma damage → chronic hypoxia → pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypotension → cor pulmonale → edema and death
Parenchyma damage → chronic hypercapnia → systemic vasoconstriction → systemic hypertension → left ventricular failure → death
Parenchyma damage → chronic hypoxia (↑PaO₂, ↓PaCO₂) → pulmonary vasodilatation → pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale → edema and death
Parenchyma damage → chronic hypoxia (↓PaO₂, ↑PaCO₂) → pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale → edema and death

units.title: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
units.sec: GOLD 2023 Definition, the Clinical and Pathological Type Trees, the Spirometry Diagnosis Rule, the Eight Risk Factors and the Four Clinical Features
units.guide:
COPD (p267) is defined by GOLD 2023 as chronic persistent respiratory symptoms from airway/alveolar abnormalities giving progressive airflow limitation, with diagnosis by symptoms plus spirometry and a clinical/pathological split into chronic bronchitis and emphysema against large airway, small airway (<2 mm), alveoli and vasculature.
Risk factors are tobacco, cooking-fuel smoke, occupational dust, vapours, fumes, other chemicals and low birth weight in preterms.
Clinical features are persistent progressive dyspnea worse on exertion, intermittent chronic cough ± sputum, recurrent LRTI and wheeze.

units.title: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
units.sec: Chronic Bronchitis against Emphysema across Definition, Pathology, Age, Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer, Chest X-ray and PFT, with the Lobule and Respiratory Unit Notes and Centriacinar Disease
units.guide:
Chronic bronchitis (p268) is the clinical disease of cough with sputum ≥3 months/year for ≥2 years, aged 40–45, with copious sputum, hypoxia → cyanosis and RV failure → edema (blue bloater), type II failure, cor pulmonale, prominent vessels and a large heart, and normal TLC and DLCO.
Emphysema is the pathological disease of dilatation distal to the terminal bronchiole with wall destruction, aged 50–75, with severe dyspnea, ↓PCO₂, cachexia, Hoover sign, hyper resonance, pursed lips (pink puffer), type I failure, hyperinflation with a small heart, and raised TLC/RV with reduced DLCO.
The functional unit is the secondary pulmonary lobule and the respiratory unit is everything distal to the terminal bronchiole; centriacinar disease is the most common, in smokers, upper lobe.

units.title: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
units.sec: Panacinar, Paraseptal and Blank Irregular Emphysema, the Protease-Antiprotease Theory, the SERPINA-1 Alleles with PiMM and PiZZ, and the Spontaneous Pneumothorax Note
units.guide:
Panacinar emphysema (p269) affects the entire acinus below 45 years in non-smokers, in the basilar lower lobe, with vasculitis, liver disease and bronchiectasis from α-1 antitrypsin deficiency; paraseptal disease affects the young male smoker and gives spontaneous pneumothorax; irregular disease is printed with a blank characteristics cell.
The protease-antiprotease flow has α-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA-1 gene) inhibiting neutrophil elastase, so deficiency raises elastase activity and destroys extracellular matrix; the alleles are m, Z and Null, with PiMM normal and PiZZ the commonest disease form.
The pneumothorax note lists paraseptal change, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and 'lymphangioma hematosis'.

units.title: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
units.sec: Large Airway Disease of Chronic Bronchitis against Asthma, Small Airway Disease of Emphysema, and the Driving-Pressure Physiology of Forced Exhalation
units.guide:
Chronic bronchitis (p270) is large airway disease with neutrophils in sputum, squamous metaplasia, no basement membrane thickening, ↑macrophages and CD8 cells, goblet hyperplasia and mucous hypersecretion, with only a little smooth muscle increase and so no hyperresponsive symptoms.
Against asthma the note table gives mild vs severe bronchospasm, increased mucus in both, epithelial necrosis absent vs present and squamous metaplasia present vs absent.
Emphysema is small airway disease with exudate, a thickened inflammatory wall, peribronchial fibrosis, lymphoid follicles and disrupted alveolar attachments → ↓ERP → easily inflatable alveoli → ↑TLC and ↑RV; DP = IPP + ERP, and forceful exhalation raises IPP with falling ERP so DP < AP, collapsing airways and trapping air.

units.title: The Alveolar DLCO Split, the Hypoxia to Cor Pulmonale Chain, Emphysematous PFT with Reversibility Testing, the GOLD Grades and the ABE Tool
units.sec: The Alveolar DLCO Split, the Hypoxia to Cor Pulmonale Chain, Emphysematous PFT with Reversibility Testing, the GOLD Grades and the ABE Tool
units.guide:
DLCO is normal with parenchymal chronic bronchitis and reduced with the emphysematous alveolo-capillary unit (p271), and parenchymal damage drives chronic hypoxia (↓PaO₂, ↑PaCO₂) → pulmonary vasoconstriction → pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale → edema or death.
Emphysema gives FEV₁ reduced with normal FVC and a reduced ratio; a ratio <0.7 sends the patient to reversibility testing, where FEV₁ rising 200 mL or 12% means asthma and no response means COPD, and post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.7 confirms the diagnosis.
GOLD 1 is ≥80%, GOLD 2 <80%, GOLD 3 <50% and GOLD 4 <30%; ≥2 exacerbations or 1 hospitalization a year defines group E; oral glucocorticoids raise side effects and lower benefits.

units.title: Inhaled Corticosteroid Indications and Contraindications, Group E against Groups A and B, LABA and LAMA Examples, and the Follow-up Treatment Flowchart
units.sec: Inhaled Corticosteroid Indications and Contraindications, Group E against Groups A and B, LABA and LAMA Examples, and the Follow-up Treatment Flowchart
units.guide:
Inhaled corticosteroids (p272) are indicated for blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/μL, ≥2 moderate exacerbations a year, concomitant asthma or asthma hospitalisation, and contraindicated by repeated pneumonia, eosinophils <100 cells/μL or a history of tuberculosis, with 2019 guidance to reduce steroid use; in asthma the pair is ICS + formoterol.
Initial treatment gives group E LABA + LAMA ± ICS when eosinophils are ≥300, group A LABA/LAMA and group B LABA + LAMA, with LABA as formoterol or indacaterol and LAMA as tiotropium.
Follow-up moves dyspnea from LABA/LAMA to LABA + LAMA, and exacerbations through eosinophils <300 to LAMA + LABA or >300 to LAMA + LABA + ICS, then roflumilast for chronic bronchitis with FEV₁ <50% or azithromycin for smoking/emphysema.

units.title: Long Term Oxygen Therapy, LVRS and the BODE Index, the Exacerbation Definition, its Three Causes and the Printed Treatment Bundle
units.sec: Long Term Oxygen Therapy, LVRS and the BODE Index, the Exacerbation Definition, its Three Causes and the Printed Treatment Bundle
units.guide:
Long term oxygen therapy (p273) runs 15–16 hours a day for PaO₂ <55 mm Hg, or 55–60 mm Hg with polycythemia or right heart failure, and LVRS is contraindicated below FEV₁ 20%.
The BODE index is BMI, obstructive ventilatory defect, dyspnea and exercise capacity; an exacerbation is dyspnea and/or cough with sputum for <14 days with systemic inflammation, caused by pneumonia, pulmonary embolism or heart failure.
Treatment is nebulization, IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, salbutamol plus ipratropium, MgSO₄, non-invasive then invasive ventilation, antibiotics for 5 days, oral steroids for 7 days and ICS for recurrent exacerbations, with no role for methylxanthines.
